title: Faith That Acts, Love Without Favorites
overview: James challenges a community that favors the rich over the poor, then argues that faith which never turns into action is not living faith at all.

parts.label: Best seats for the rich (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: A visitor with a gold ring and fine clothes gets a good seat, while a poor visitor is told to stand or sit on the floor. James says this sorting makes them judges with evil motives, whether the scene is a worship gathering or, as some scholars think, a church meeting to settle disputes.

parts.label: God's view of the poor (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: James reminds them that God has chosen people the world counts as poor to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom he promised. Yet they have shamed the poor, while it is the rich, likely mostly outsiders, who exploit them, drag them into court and insult the name of Christ they bear.

parts.label: The law of love and mercy (vv. 8-13)
parts.note: The 'royal law' is the command in Leviticus 19:18 to love your neighbor as yourself, and favoritism breaks it, because one God gave every command and you cannot keep some while excusing yourself on others. James asks them to live knowing they will be judged by a law that sets people free, where those who show no mercy receive none, but mercy wins over judgment.

parts.label: Kind words, empty hands (vv. 14-20)
parts.note: Telling a cold, hungry person to keep warm and eat well while giving them nothing helps no one, and James says faith that never acts is just as dead. Believing that God is one, the core belief from Deuteronomy 6:4, is good, James says. But even demons believe it, and it only makes them shudder.

parts.label: Abraham's test (vv. 21-24)
parts.note: James points to Genesis 22, where God tells Abraham to offer his son Isaac as a sacrifice and then stops him before he does. For James this act brought Abraham's earlier trust (Genesis 15:6) to completion, which leads to his much debated line in verse 24 that a person is counted righteous, or 'justified' in some translations, by what they do and not by faith alone.

parts.label: Rahab and the closing picture (vv. 25-26)
parts.note: Rahab, a woman of Jericho called a prostitute, hid two Israelite spies and sent them out by another route, and she and her family were spared when Israel destroyed the city (Joshua 2 and 6). James ends with an image: a body without its spirit, or breath, is dead, and so is faith that does nothing.

disagreement: Paul writes that people are made right with God by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28), and Christians differ on how James fits: many Protestants read James as saying good deeds show that faith is real, while Catholic and Orthodox Christians tend to read him as saying faith and deeds together share in being made right with God, with both seen as gifts of God's grace and not a way to earn it.
think: Can you tell what someone truly believes from how they treat people, or are there things about belief that actions can never show?
